body.text: A persistent problem for the custodians of any established order is to reconcile the immediate demands of their own kind with the long-term health and welfare of the order as a whole.

Consider, for example, the case of Michael Stutchbury and schooling. Stutchbury heads the Centre for Independent Studies, a prominent think tank funded by the big end of town. He came to the job recently after thirteen years as editor-in-chief of the Financial Review (a record) that followed a stint as economics editor at the similarly minded Australian.

At the CIS Stutchbury inherited an interest in schooling, represented most recently by two reports, one on “the classroom crisis,” the other on “Australia’s teacher professional knowledge gap.” Both rely on tendentious surveys; their “findings” come as no surprise to anyone. Both tread well-worn paths; both focus on teaching rather than learning; both assume that “learning” is to do with heads not hearts (and certainly not hands); both run a line descending from the Gillard “education revolution” of 2007–13 (make teachers more “effective” and up the OECD ladder we’ll go). One shows no interest in why students “misbehave”; the other assumes that teachers teach the way they do not in response to the circumstances of their work but because they have the wrong ideas in their heads. Both hanker after schooling’s status quo ante, and so does Stutchbury. As he put it in warm endorsement of the classroom crisis report, what we need is schools with clear rules and expectations, desks facing the front, and teachers who are “the authority in the classroom.”

Stutchbury’s unqualified endorsements of the two reports are as surprising in what they don’t say as what they do. There is no speculation about the relationship between schooling and right-wing populism, in Australia as elsewhere attributable in part to the resentments of those who as kids were humiliated at school — Hillary Clinton’s “deplorables.” There is no reference to rising anxieties about “social cohesion,” despite the fact that just about any religion, denomination, sect or persuasion can set up a school in Australia and enrol its own kids. There is not even a passing reference to the fact that Australian schools are among the most socially segregated in the OECD world.

Perhaps most surprising of all: neither of the CIS reports nor Stutchbury’s endorsements of them mention the rethink of schooling and its social role now under way in circles adjacent to their own. In the run-up to the last federal election, for example, the Association of Heads of Independent Schools was bitterly critical of “policy-makers” who “need to be reminded about how children learn” and called for “a refreshed narrative about the purposes of Australian schooling,” while in a similar vein but on a very much larger scale the world’s most influential think-tank on matters educational, the OECD, has been developing a new “vision” for schooling, arguing that the schools of the future must go beyond supplying what the economy wants to encourage “human flourishing.”

Why are the CIS’s eyes closed to the shifting social world around schooling, its ears deaf to those spelling out the implications? Why is it deaf and blind to the kind of thing the sponsors of the CIS might expect to be told about? And why is an economic radical an out-and-out educational reactionary?
Some speculations, in rough order from the obvious and immediate to the enduring and fundamental:

1. In fighting the battle it has lost sight of the war. The CIS is deeply committed to a struggle against what it sees as schooling’s woke/progressive/cultural-Marxist culture. One-time CIS education analyst Jennifer Buckingham is now head of the NSW Education Department’s Centre for Evaluation and Statistics, intellectual engine-room for the department’s all-encompassing “explicit instruction” campaign. Buckingham’s predecessor in that position, Jenny Donovan, is now head of the Australian Education Research Organisation, or AERO, a handsomely funded propagator of “evidence-based” and “direct” instruction. Both dogmas are heavily backed by the Murdoch media, former employer of both Stutchbury and his predecessor at the CIS, Tom Switzer. The CIS is thinking tactics, not strategy.

2. They just don’t get it. The “scientific” branch of the discipline of psychology has suffused Australian educational thinking since the 1930s, first via IQ theory, then through its derivative, the “effective teaching” doctrine, and now via another derivative, cognitive science, the science of learning according to AERO et al. It isn’t the science of learning at all; it is just one of the sciences trying to understand human growth and learning, generally disdained by the others for its focus on cognition to the exclusion of emotions, relationships and context.

Psychology and its offspring focus on the behaviour of individuals, teachers mainly, and find there both the source of schooling’s problems and the hope of its salvation. They pay no attention to the organisation of the work of learning or to the larger structures of schooling — funding that is the inverse of need, for example, or a governance system that grants independence to some but imposes top-down bureaucratic control on others. In the absence of a wider view schools appear to be just places where kids go to be taught rather than parts of a large and consequential institution that allocates futures, shapes minds, and makes the established order seem both fair and necessary.

A problem within the problem for the CIS is that those who do take the wider view and try to figure out the policy implications are mostly of that wretched progressive/radical/cultural–Marxist left — Tom Greenwell and Chris Bonnor and their case for a modified sector system, for example, or Geoff Masters and his explanation of how curriculum can and should be organised around each student’s progress, needs and interests.

3. They don’t want to get it. Only just below the surface of the CIS’s thinking on schooling is the instinct for control, for the exercise of authority by those who are up and on the inside over those who are neither. So far as schools are concerned, that includes kids: why should they sit up straight and do as they’re told? Because they’re kids. They’re not at school to flourish; they’re there to be instructed, directly and explicitly, for their own good, particularly if they’re of the working and dependent classes.

Those disorderly classrooms of the CIS report aren’t in the gated communities patronised by the readers of the Fin Review and the membership of the CIS, and nor are the teachers who don’t know their “learning science”; they’re out there where there are no towering atriums or harbour views or white-napkin lunches. What authority out there needs is a bit up of stiffening up. Manning Clark reckoned that the prime ministers of Australia belonged to one or other of two categories, the enlargers of life, or the punishers and straighteners. There are enlargers among the custodians of the established order — David Gonski, perhaps — but Michael Stutchbury and the CIS don’t frighten easily. They’re straighteners, first and last.
